title: Relational Structural Causal Models
claim: Answering a query about an unseen combination of objects requires transferring knowledge from training structures to a differently structured target.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right with plus and arrow; each stacked scene, skeleton, graph
description: The figure has two yellow banners, Training and Evaluation, over three dashed rounded panels: Slip Lane, City Block and T-Junction. A plus sign joins the two training panels, and an arrow leads from them to the evaluation panel. Each panel is built the same way. At top is a cartoon traffic scene with traffic lights, pedestrians and cars, labeled s, p and c. Beside it is a skeleton graph with green signal nodes, blue pedestrian nodes and orange car nodes. Small white bubbles sit on the edges, and red dotted outlines mark cars with similar neighborhoods. At bottom is a black-dot causal graph with nodes such as s1.W, p1.X and c1.B. The training panels are annotated with data P(v_ρ). The evaluation panel carries a boxed query, P(c1.b=1 | do(s1.w=1)). The eye goes first to the colorful skeleton graphs and the arrow between the panels.
caption: A schematic for the problem of relational identification across varying traffic scenes, following the schema in Ex. [ref]. Each panel shows: (i) a relational skeleton \(\rho\) representing a particular combination of signals (\(s\)), pedestrians (\(p\)), and cars (\(c\)), (ii) the corresponding causal graph \(\bar{\G}_{\rho}\), and (iii) the available data or the query of interest. The goal is to use data from the source skeletons \(\rho_A\) and \(\rho_B\) to answer a query about the target skeleton \(\rho_B\). In any \(\rho\), an edge \((s_i,p_j)\) indicates that signal \(s_i\) controls pedestrian \(p_j\); an edge \((s_i,c_j)\) indicates that signal \(s_i\) controls car \(c_j\); and an edge \((p_i,c_j)\) indicates that pedestrian \(p_i\) is in the path of car \(c_j\). A bubble marks the second tuple element. Cars with similar relational neighborhoods skeletons are circumscribed by similar shapes (red dotted line).
abstract: An artificial intelligence must have a model of its environment that is causal, supporting reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, and also combinatorial, supporting generalization to unseen combinations of objects. In this work, we formally study when and how such a model can be learned. We develop relational structural causal models, extending structural causal models (Pearl 2009) to settings where objects and their relations vary. First, we show how answers to not only causal but also observational queries about unseen combinations of objects can not be identified without further assumptions. To enable such identification--including in the presence of unobserved confounding--we define relational causal graphs and derive symbolic identification criteria. Finally, we propose relational neural causal models, a provably correct approach that outperforms non-relational baselines on simulated traffic scenes with varying cars, signals, and pedestrians.
